claims.text: The baseline high-entropy alloy is designed as an intermediate material for plasma-facing reactor components.
The baseline alloy is optimized for high-temperature strength and moderate thermal conductivity.
Approximately 3 at.% Ag will be added to the baseline alloy by vacuum arc melting and rapid solidification.
Adding approximately 3 at.% Ag under the proposed processing conditions will produce an evenly dispersed, nanoscale Ag-rich phase.
The dispersed Ag-rich phase will coalesce into an interconnected or percolated network.
The Ag-rich phase will be localized along grain boundaries and interdendritic regions.
The interconnected Ag-rich phase will act as a thermal bridge between lower-thermal-conductivity matrix regions.
Silver's high intrinsic thermal conductivity will allow the Ag-rich network to enhance electron-mediated heat transfer through the alloy microstructure.
Rapid solidification will maintain the Ag-rich phase as a nanoscale dispersion.
The nanoscale Ag dispersion will leave the mechanical load-bearing matrix largely unaffected.
The Ag-modified alloy will retain yield strength and fracture toughness under the proposed reactor-relevant conditions.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Ag-modified alloy will exhibit a 15–20% increase in thermal conductivity.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Ag-modified alloy will incur no more than a 5% reduction in yield strength or fracture toughness.
The predicted benefits will hold during cyclic thermal loading from approximately 200°C to 800°C.
The 200°C to 800°C cyclic-loading range simulates plasma-facing reactor service conditions.
Operation significantly above 800°C may compromise structural integrity or thermal benefits.
Prolonged thermal cycling may coarsen the Ag-rich phase or disrupt its interconnected network.
Ag-phase coarsening or network breakdown may reduce the alloy's thermal benefit or structural integrity.
